title: Lessons for a quarter and the post office band
summary: Lessons cost 25 cents; he played in the post office brass band, rehearsed twice a week, and mentions service years.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: That's right. But under Professor Chalini I enjoyed my music very much. As a matter of fact I didn't get as much out of it as I should have or I could have because at that particular time, being the youngster you know you always come home from school, throw your books on the couch or the machine and you go out and play some ball, football or baseball or basketball or something of that particular nature, until I was reminded of the fact that I had to go to lessons. And the very good thing about it, lessons was I would say very expensive. I thought they were very reasonable.

Twenty-five cents a lesson. Twenty-five cents a lesson, which I thought was very reasonable. Of course at that time money was scarce and for that particular time of the year and in New Orleans you didn't take, you didn't need too much money to operate or as you might say, or you didn't need too much money to live. And we got to learn our instruments pretty well while we was invited to play with the post office band. The post office had organized a band and he was the director at the time. So I was particularly fascinated by this venture because of the fact I would be out in the streets just like the rest of the fellas was playing. Sort of a brass band? Yes, that's what it was. Uh-huh. And usually on anniversary days and memorial days we'd get out to the post office and play and it was particularly exciting.
You played B flat clarinet I guess?
Did you ever play E flat?

No. Well the only time I played E flat was in service. I played in service for about four years during the last war from 1942 to 1946. And but speaking about this old post office band, I was particularly interested in it and really enjoyed it for the simple reason that we used to rehearse twice a week. And we used to rehearse at different fellas' homes, you know.
Did most of the fellas work at the post office?

Well I'd say about half of them, or maybe a little more than half, worked at the post office. Well I think that was a general idea to comprise a band with members of the post office. And well I got a big bang out of it for the simple reason. We'd rehearse twice a week and we'd have such a good time after the rehearsals. And that's the thing I always looked forward to was the food and drinks afterwards, you know. And it was the same condition. I guess I could have been a heck of a lot more advanced than I was if it wasn't for the good times that were centered around that particular time. I could remember another incident where I was working with a cousin of mine at the time. He was a saxophone player. His name was Dejean. Did you know Dejean? Harold Dejean? Yes. I've seen him in the, he played a parade a couple of weeks ago. Al Crocise has his own band now. Oh is that right? I haven't seen him.
